The pattern of discontinuities shown in Figure 7-13a is typical for sedimentary rock, such as limestone, sandstone, and shale, that has been deposited in bedded layers and later uplifted by geologic processes. The orientation of the discontinuities in Figure 7-13a is roughly parallel to the rock slope face, but they do not daylight at the slope face. In such a configuration the rock slope face is expected to remain stable. In contrast, Figure 7-13b shows a rock slope with discontinuities that daylight at the slope face. With such orientation of discontinuities, a potential for rock slope failures exists.

Figure 7-13c shows a rock slope with generally favorable bedding in that the discontinuities dip into the rock slope and there is little potential for rock to slide out of the slope face. However, blocks of rock at the slope face may become instable when discontinuities daylight at the slope face. The potential for the development of such conditions are increased if blasting was performed during slope excavation.

A rock slope configuration that illustrates the conditions for the toppling of rock columns is shown in Figure 7-13d. Toppling becomes a risk for rock with relatively thin bedding with steeply dipping discontinuities. The stability of rock columns can degrade relatively quickly if water seeps readily into the discontinuities from surface water runoff and increases the rate of weathering. In regions with frequent freeze-thaw cycles the rate of degradation may accelerate further because the frozen water can cause the rock columns to separate.

Sandstone and shale are often found with near-horizontal bedding. Excavation of such a bedding sequence generally results in a shale layers that weather faster than sandstone. In such conditions layers of sandstone may be undermined and form ledges that are prone to fracturing and failure. Such a condition is illustrated in Figure 7-14a.

Weak rock slopes with closely spaced impersistent joints may fail along a circular or noncircular surface much like a soil slope as shown in Figure 7-14b.

An assessment of the potential for one of the above modes of failure to develop often requires a geologic investigation, field mapping of discontinuities, stereographic projection of geologic data, and an evaluation of rock strength.
key_points: Rock slope failure occurs due to propagation of discontinuities forming blocks/wedges/columns, or rock fall of already-separated material.
Discontinuities that do not daylight at the slope face generally indicate a stable slope; daylighting discontinuities indicate failure potential.
Toppling risk is highest for thin-bedded rock with steeply dipping discontinuities, especially in freeze-thaw environments.
Sandstone over shale sequences can produce undermined ledges prone to fracture after excavation.
Weak rock with closely spaced impersistent joints may fail along circular/noncircular surfaces similar to soil slopes.
Assessment requires geologic investigation, field mapping, stereographic projection, and rock strength evaluation.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying which mode of rock slope failure is relevant to a specific site based on discontinuity patterns and rock type.

sections.title: Mechanics of a Sliding Block
sections.summary: Presents the fundamental force equilibrium for a sliding rock block, defining weight components normal (FN) and parallel (FS) to the sliding plane as functions of the dip angle ΨP. Establishes the factor of safety against sliding assuming no pore pressure, and notes that positive pore pressure reduces effective normal stress and the factor of safety.
sections.body:
The mechanics of a sliding block are central to two types of rock slope stability analyses. Considering the rock slope depicted in Figure 7-15, the weight of the block ABC is represented by force W, which acts through the block's centroid. The component of W that acts perpendicular to the sliding plane AC is FN. The component of W that acts parallel to the sliding plane AC is FS. The relationship of these three forces is defined by the angle, or dip, of the sliding plane (ΨP) with respect to the horizontal plane.

The factor of safety against sliding on plane AC is calculated as shown in Figure 7-15. This solution assumes no pore pressure is acting on the sliding plane. Positive pore pressure will reduce the effective normal stress, shear strength, and the factor of safety.
key_points: Block weight W is decomposed into normal (FN) and parallel (FS) components relative to the sliding plane, governed by dip angle ΨP.
Factor of safety against sliding is the ratio of resisting to driving forces along the sliding plane.
No pore pressure is assumed in the basic formulation; pore pressure reduces effective normal stress and lowers the factor of safety.
This sliding block model is foundational for both plane failure and wedge failure analyses.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing a basic factor of safety calculation for a rock block sliding on a planar surface with no pore pressure.

sections.title: Plane Failure
sections.summary: Describes plane failure as a specific case of the sliding block model, noting it is relatively rare due to strict geometric requirements. Emphasizes its instructional value for understanding wedge failure mechanics and introduces the conditions and orientation terminology needed for plane failure analysis.
sections.body: The rock slope with a sliding block shown in Figure 7-15 is a simple version of a plane failure. It is not a type of failure that is often encountered because the conditions for its development rarely occur. However, the mechanics of a plane failure also apply to the more frequently encountered wedge failure. For this reason, it is instructive to further consider plane failures.
key_points: Plane failure is a simplified and relatively rare rock slope failure mode requiring specific geometric conditions.
Understanding plane failure mechanics is essential because the same principles apply to the more common wedge failure.
Two subsections cover orientation terminology and the four geometric conditions required for plane failure.
sections.applicability: Applies as a container section when studying plane failure mechanics and their relationship to wedge failure analysis.

sections.title: Sloped Surface Orientation Terms
sections.summary: Defines the three key geometric terms used to describe planar orientations in rock slope analysis: dip (Ψ), dip direction/dip azimuth (α), and strike. Establishes that strike is perpendicular to dip direction, providing the vocabulary needed for plane and wedge failure assessments.
sections.body:
A discussion of plane failure requires the definition of three terms that are used to describe the orientation of sloped planes such as a slope face or a potential failure surface. The dip (Ψ) of a sloped plane is the inclination of that surface as measured from a horizontal plane, as shown in Figure 7-16. The dip direction or dip azimuth (α) is the direction of the horizontal trace of the line of dip measured clockwise from north.

Often the term strike is used to describe the orientation of a sloped plane. It is the direction of a line that is formed by an intersection of the sloped plane with an imaginary horizontal plane. The orientation of the strike of a sloped surface is perpendicular to the dip direction of the sloped surface.
key_points: Dip (Ψ) is the inclination of a plane measured from horizontal.
Dip direction or dip azimuth (α) is measured clockwise from north along the horizontal trace of the dip line.
Strike is the direction of intersection of the sloped plane with a horizontal plane; it is perpendicular to the dip direction.
These three terms are fundamental vocabulary for rock slope discontinuity characterization.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever describing or analyzing the geometric orientation of rock discontinuities, slope faces, or failure planes.

sections.title: General Conditions for Plane Failure
sections.summary: Lists the four geometric conditions that must all be satisfied for plane failure to occur, per Hoek and Bray (1981): the failure plane must strike nearly parallel to the slope face, daylight at the slope face (ΨP < ΨF), have a dip exceeding the friction angle (φ′ < ΨP), and release surfaces with negligible resistance must exist at the lateral boundaries.
sections.body:
For sliding to occur on a single plane the four conditions must be satisfied (Hoek and Bray 1981):
1. The plane on which sliding occurs must strike nearly parallel (i.e., within about 20º) to the slope face.
2. The failure plane must daylight in the slope face (i.e., intersect the slope face). Therefore, the dip of the failure plane (ΨP) must be less than the dip of the slope face, ΨF. That is, ΨP < ΨF.
3. The dip of the failure plane must be greater than the angle of friction at the failure plane. That is, φʹ < ΨF.
4. Release surfaces that provide negligible resistance to sliding must be present in the rock mass to define the lateral boundaries of the slide.
The relative positions of the planes defined by ΨF, ΨP, and φʹ are shown in Figure 7-17a. The release surfaces associated with a sliding plane are shown in Figure 7-17b.
key_points: Failure plane strike must be within ~20° of the slope face strike.
Failure plane must daylight at slope face: ΨP < ΨF.
Failure plane dip must exceed friction angle: φ′ < ΨP.
Lateral release surfaces with negligible sliding resistance must exist to define slide boundaries.
All four conditions must be met simultaneously for plane failure to develop.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing whether geometric conditions at a rock slope site are sufficient for plane failure to occur.

sections.title: Plane Failure Analyses
sections.summary: Covers the factor of safety calculation for plane failure including the effects of a tension crack (above or below the slope crest) that may contain water. Defines uplift force U at the failure plane and water force V in the tension crack, as shown in Figure 7-18. Notes that computer programs improve analytical efficiency over hand calculations.
sections.body:
Rock slopes analyzed for plane failure can also consider the presence of a tension crack, which may contain water. The crack may be located either above or below the slope crest as shown in Figure 7-18. The uplift force applied by water at the failure plane is designated as U. The force applied by water in the tension crack is designated as V. The factor of safety for such conditions can be calculated using the equation presented in Figure 7-18.

Further details regarding the stability analyses of sliding planes are described in the FHWA (1998) and by Hoek and Bray (1981). While such analyses can be practically performed using hand calculations, analytical efficiency can be significantly improved by use of computer programs.
key_points: Plane failure analysis can incorporate tension cracks located either above or below the slope crest.
Water in the tension crack introduces force V; water on the failure plane introduces uplift force U.
Both U and V reduce the factor of safety by decreasing effective normal stress and adding a driving force.
The factor of safety equation accounting for U and V is presented graphically in Figure 7-18.
Computer programs significantly improve efficiency over hand calculations for these analyses.
sections.applicability: Applies when computing the factor of safety for plane failure in rock slopes that may have tension cracks and/or water pressure on the failure plane.

sections.title: Wedge Failure
sections.summary: Describes wedge failure analysis for rock slopes where two intersecting discontinuity planes (Plane A and Plane B) define a sliding wedge. Introduces the wedge factor K relating wedge factor of safety FW to equivalent plane failure conditions, and notes that cohesion and water pressure require more complex analysis available in FHWA (1998) and Hoek and Bray (1981).
sections.body:
The rock slope with a sliding wedge shown in Figure 7-19 is similar to a sliding plane, but the presence of Plane A and Plane B make it possible to model a geometry that is encountered in the field more frequently.

The convention adopted in the FHWA (1998) and by Hoek and Bray (1981) is that the release surface designated as Plane A is the flatter of the two release surfaces. The steeper release surface is designated as Plane B. These two surfaces intersect along the line of intersection.

As with a plane failure, there are certain geometrical requirements for wedge failure to occur. Specifically, ΨFi > Ψi > φʹ, where ΨFi is the inclination of the slope face as measured at right angles to the line of intersection, Ψi is the dip of the line of intersection and φʹ is the average friction angle of Plane A and Plane B. Note that ΨFi is not the same as ΨF unless the dip direction of the line of intersection is the same as the dip direction of the slope face (Hoek and Bray 1981).

The factor of safety of the wedge in Figure 7-19 may be determined by assuming that sliding is resisted only by friction at the surface of Plane A and Plane B. With this simplifying assumption, the resisting forces on these planes can be determined by calculation of the normal forces RA and RB on each plane, as illustrated in Figure 7-20a. The component forces of the weight of the wedge perpendicular and parallel to the line of intersection are shown in Figure 7-20b.

Hoek and Bray (1981) relate the factor of safety against wedge failure (FW) to that for a slope with a face that is inclined at ΨFi and a failure plane that is inclined at Ψi by a wedge factor K. This wedge factor can be graphically determined using a figure provided in both the FHWA (1998) and Hoek and Bray (1981).

The analysis of a wedge failure for which cohesion or water are present is more complicated than for a wedge failure in which only the friction angle at the failure planes is considered. Both the FHWA (1998) and by Hoek and Bray (1981) discuss this analytical process in detail. Such an analysis can also be performed efficiently using computer programs.
key_points: Wedge failure involves two intersecting release planes (Plane A = flatter, Plane B = steeper) forming a sliding wedge.
Geometric requirement: ΨFi > Ψi > φ′, where ΨFi is slope face inclination perpendicular to the line of intersection and Ψi is the dip of that line.
ΨFi differs from ΨF unless the line of intersection dip direction matches the slope face dip direction.
Basic analysis assumes friction only on Plane A and Plane B; normal forces RA and RB are computed from wedge weight components.
Wedge factor K relates FW to equivalent plane failure factor of safety; K is determined graphically.
Cohesion and water pressure require more detailed analysis; computer programs are recommended.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating factor of safety against wedge failure for a rock slope with two intersecting discontinuity planes.

sections.title: Toppling Failure
sections.summary: Explains toppling failure mechanics for rock columns where the center of gravity lies on the slope-face side, creating eccentric loading and tensile stress on the back face. Notes that toppling analyses are significantly more complex than plane or block failure and that hand calculation methods (FHWA 1998) may have limited applicability to field conditions.
sections.body:
For a column of rock to be subject to toppling failure, the center of gravity of the column must be located on the side of the column at the slope face. In this way, the column is loaded eccentrically. Such loading creates tensile stress on the side of the column away from the slope face, as shown in Figure 7-21. If the tensile capacity of the column is exceeded, failure can ensue.

Analyses of rock toppling can be significantly more complicated than those for plane failure or block failure. A method for hand calculations is described in FHWA (1998) but such a procedure may have limited applicability to actual field conditions.
key_points: Toppling occurs when the center of gravity of a rock column is on the slope-face side, creating eccentric loading.
Eccentric loading generates tensile stress on the back face of the column; failure occurs when tensile capacity is exceeded.
Toppling analyses are substantially more complex than plane or block failure analyses.
Hand calculation methods from FHWA (1998) exist but have limited applicability to real field conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing the risk of toppling failure for rock columns with steeply dipping, thin-bedded discontinuities at a slope face.

sections.title: Circular Failure
sections.summary: Addresses circular or noncircular failure of weak rock slopes with closely spaced impersistent joints, analogous to soil slope failure. Cautions that weak intact rock can still have significant cohesion, that cohesive strength is difficult to measure accurately, and that zones of stronger rock behind weaker zones may shift the location of the critical failure surface.
sections.body: As described in section 7-10.1, if a rock slope consists of weak material with closely spaced, impersistent joints, then the slope may fail along a circular or noncircular surface much as a soil slope. Analyses of these types of failures can be performed using the methods previously discussed for the stability of soil slopes. However, it should be noted that even weak intact rock can exhibit significant cohesive strength. An accurate assessment of the actual cohesive strength may be difficult to make. It is also important to realize that zones of relatively strong rock may exist behind zones of relatively weak rock. The presence of the strong rock zones may significantly affect the location of the critical failure surface.
key_points: Weak rock with closely spaced impersistent joints can fail along circular or noncircular surfaces similar to soil slopes.
Soil slope stability methods are applicable for these analyses.
Even weak intact rock may have significant cohesive strength that is difficult to measure accurately.
Zones of stronger rock behind weaker rock can significantly influence the location of the critical failure surface.
sections.applicability: Applies when analyzing failure of weak or closely jointed rock slopes where failure mode resembles soil slope circular failure.

sections.title: Rock Slope Stabilization and Protection
sections.summary: Introduces the range of measures available to mitigate hazards from unstable rock slopes, varying from simple to complex in terms of required analytical expertise, construction skill, and expense. Serves as a container section for subsections covering reinforcement, shotcrete, buttresses, drains, rock removal, rock fall protection, and rock sheds/tunnels.
sections.body: Several measures can be taken to mitigate the hazards presented by unstable rock slopes. These measures vary from the relatively simple to those which require considerable analytical expertise, construction skill, and expense.
key_points: Stabilization measures range from simple (scaling, drains) to complex (active anchors, catch fences, rock sheds).
Categories include rock reinforcement, rock removal, and protective barriers.
Selection of appropriate measure depends on the failure mode, site conditions, and cost.
sections.applicability: Applies as an overview container when selecting and designing rock slope stabilization or protection measures.

sections.title: Stabilization and Protection Options
sections.summary: Summarizes the three primary categories of rock slope stabilization measures — rock reinforcement, rock removal, and protective barriers — and references Figure 7-22 which enumerates specific options within each category per FHWA (1998).
sections.body: The range of stabilization measures that are typically available include rock reinforcement, rock removal and protective barriers. A range of options is available under each of these categories as shown in Figure 7-22.
key_points: Three primary categories of stabilization: rock reinforcement, rock removal, and protective barriers.
Figure 7-22 (after FHWA 1998) enumerates specific options within each category.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying and comparing available stabilization and protection options for an unstable rock slope.

sections.title: Reinforcement
sections.summary: Covers passive anchors (rock bolts/dowels, soil nails) and active anchors (stressed bar or strand tendons) for rock slope stabilization. Describes installation methods, typical bar sizes (No. 8–No. 11), tensile capacities (35–500+ kips for strand), grout vs. resin bonding, corrosion protection, and references FHWA GEC No. 7 and GEC No. 4. Includes electrochemical limits for corrosive environments.
sections.body:
Anchors have been used for many years to stabilize both soil and rock slopes. In general, anchors can be classified as passive or active. A passive anchor that is frequently used for top-down excavation stabilization is the soil nail. For rock slope stabilization it may be referred to as a rock bolt or dowel. It typically comprises a steel tendon in the form of an all-thread bar that is centered within a drill hole. A cement grout is installed in the drill hole to bond the tendon to the adjacent soil or rock. Grout is usually placed by tremie from the distal end to the anchor head. Typically, such holes are drilled at a declination of about 15° or more below the horizontal plane to prevent spilling of the grout at the excavated face.

The steel bars used for these applications typically exhibit a tensile capacity of at least 75 ksi. Higher capacity bars are readily available. Typical bar diameters correspond to standard reinforcement steel sizes of #8 (i.e. 1.0-inch nominal diameter) to #11 (i.e. 1.41-inch nominal diameter). Resistance to bar corrosion is typically provided by an epoxy coating or galvanization. The grout that surrounds the bar can also provide some protection against corrosion, but the grout is subject to cracking and may not provide complete coverage.

Different types of liquid resins are manufactured for use with rock anchors as an alternative to cement grout. Resin cartridges include a hardener that can be selected to provide a range of hardening times. The cartridges are inserted into the drill hole and then followed by insertion of the steel bar tendon. The tendon is then spun at a prescribed rate to mix the resin and hardening agent and to distribute the mixture to both bar and rock surfaces. Unfortunately, there is some skepticism within the ground anchor contracting industry that resins can be consistently distributed to rock and tendon surfaces and can reliably provide requisite bond capacities. Also, resins do not provide the same level of corrosion protection as does cement grout.

The FHWA has published several manuals on the design of soil nail structures. The current version is Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 7 (FHWA 2015). This manual should be consulted in the design of passive anchors for rock stabilization applications.

A passive anchor does not impart a stabilization force to the adjacent rock or soil until the rock or soil tends to displace. At that point the passive anchor provides a resisting force. In contrast, an active anchor is stressed as part of its installation process. Such anchors may comprise steel bars like a soil nail. However, if a particularly long anchor or one with high tensile capacity is required, then steel strand tendons may be indicated. The installation of such an active anchor is similar to that of a passive anchor. First, a hole for the anchor is drilled and then the strand is inserted and centered within the hole. Next, the strand is grouted, but only for a certain length of the strand starting from the distal end. A length between the top of the grouted section and the anchor head is left unbonded. The reason for the unbonded section is that this portion of the tendon must be left to strain under a design stressing load to provide an active force at the anchor head. This force is transferred to a loading plate or block that is secured against the rock slope face. In this way the active force can be used to stabilize a large rock plane, wedge or unstable columns. This is perhaps the most important distinction between an active anchor and a passive anchor. Unlike a passive anchor, an active anchor does not depend on soil or rock movement to mobilize its strength.

The bonded length of the tendon is that portion which is grouted. The length of the bonded section is based on analyses that consider the load in the anchor and the bond strength between the grout and the adjacent soil or rock.

Steel strand tendons are typically available in configurations that provide a working tensile capacity of about 35 to 500 kips. Tendons with considerably higher capacities can be fabricated.

The design of active anchor systems is discussed in the FHWA's Geotechnical Engineering Circular No. 4 (FHWA 1999). This manual should be consulted in the design of active anchors for rock stabilization applications.

When anchors are designed for the stabilization of rock slopes, some consideration should be given to the potential for conditions that may cause steel corrosion. Such conditions often prevail in areas where coal and acidic runoff are present or where sodic and pyritic soils are found. The FHWA provides the electrochemical parameters in Table 7-8 as limits for the use of steel reinforcement in MSE structures. These limits should be considered when designing the corrosion protection for active and passive anchors.
key_points: Passive anchors (rock bolts/dowels/soil nails) mobilize resistance only when rock or soil tends to displace; active anchors are pre-stressed at installation.
Typical passive anchor bars: #8–#11 steel (1.0–1.41 in. diameter), ≥75 ksi tensile capacity; drilled at ≥15° declination to prevent grout spillage.
Active anchors use bonded + unbonded strand tendons; working capacity typically 35–500 kips; unbonded section allows pre-stressing.
Cement grout provides better corrosion protection and bond reliability than resin for rock anchors.
FHWA GEC No. 7 (FHWA 2015) governs passive anchor design; FHWA GEC No. 4 (FHWA 1999) governs active anchor design.
Corrosive environments (coal, acidic runoff, pyritic soils) require corrosion-protected anchors; Table 7-8 provides electrochemical limits.
Active anchors are superior for stabilizing large rock planes, wedges, or columns because they do not require movement to mobilize force.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing passive or active anchor reinforcement systems for rock slope stabilization, especially in potentially corrosive environments.

sections.title: Shotcrete
sections.summary: Describes shotcrete application for stabilizing rock slopes subject to raveling and dislodgement of gravel, cobbles, and boulders. Covers reinforcement with WWF or bars, anchor spacing (≤6 ft), the critical role of drainage composites to prevent delamination from water pressure or freezing, and weep hole detailing.
sections.body:
Shotcrete is essentially concrete that has little to no gravel-size particles (i.e. larger than the No. 4 sieve) that can be sprayed onto vertical and near-vertical surfaces. It is usually applied in layers to build up the total coating to a specified thickness. Both steel welded wire fabric (WWF) and bars may be used within the shotcrete to provide reinforcement.

Shotcrete can be used to stabilize rock slopes that are subject to raveling and dislodgement of gravel, cobble and boulders. It will tend to adhere to such unstable faces but it should be secured with relatively short passive anchors (i.e. soil nails, rock bolts or dowels). Otherwise, the shotcrete may delaminate from the rock slope in a short period of time. The length of the anchors can be 10 feet or less if they are not actually needed for stabilization of rock planes and wedges. If the rock slope surface is mostly unstable then the anchors should be spaced at intervals no greater than about 6 feet.

A common cause for separation of shotcrete from the face of a rock slope is the presence of water behind the shotcrete. Water frequently seeps from rock slopes, and it should be drained using a drainage composite. Drainage is especially important in climates where the water can freeze. Drainage composites can be successfully used behind shotcrete. The composites typically are available in a width of 4 feet. They should be installed with a coverage of 50%. A drainage grate should be installed at the base of each drainage composite strip and daylighted by a weep hole through the shotcrete.
key_points: Shotcrete contains no particles larger than No. 4 sieve and is applied in layers to vertical/near-vertical rock faces.
Must be secured with passive anchors (≤10 ft length for surface stabilization only); anchors spaced ≤6 ft on mostly unstable faces.
Water behind shotcrete is a primary cause of delamination; drainage composites must be installed.
Drainage composites (4 ft wide) should cover 50% of the shotcrete area; weep holes and drainage grates required at their base.
Drainage is especially critical in freeze-thaw climates to prevent ice-induced delamination.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing shotcrete face protection for rock slopes subject to raveling, dislodgement, or surface instability.

sections.title: Buttress
sections.summary: Describes buttresses as gravity structures providing passive resistance to rock slope displacement. Options include piled soil or rock, reinforced concrete structures, or MSE structures. Engineering analyses are analogous to gravity retaining wall design.
sections.body: Buttresses have been used for more than 1,000 years to stabilize slopes, walls and buildings. In general, a buttress is a gravity structure that provides passive resistance to displacement. For rock slope stabilization a buttress may comprise piled soil or rock, or it may be an engineered reinforced concrete structure or an MSE structure. The engineering analyses of the mass requirements of a buttress are relatively straightforward and similar to those of a gravity retaining wall.
key_points: A buttress is a gravity structure that passively resists displacement at the base of a rock slope.
Options include piled soil/rock, reinforced concrete, or MSE structures.
Mass requirement analyses are similar to gravity retaining wall design.
sections.applicability: Applies when a passive gravity structure is needed at the toe of a rock slope to resist displacement.

sections.title: Drains
sections.summary: Covers relief drains for rock slopes, which are drilled at ≥2° above horizontal (opposite to anchors) to dissipate pore pressures. Notes the practical limitation that relief drains frequently become clogged by organic material and that removal of obstructions is generally not practical.
sections.body:
Drains are often used in conjunction with rock slope reinforcement measures to counter the destabilizing effects of water that is retained behind a slope face. In general, relief drains are drilled using equipment similar to that used for anchors. However, instead of being angle below the horizontal plane relief drains are typically angle 2° or more above the horizontal plane.

An unfortunate reality of relief drains is that they often become clogged by the accumulation of organic material. Removal of the organic obstructions is generally not practical.
key_points: Relief drains are drilled at ≥2° above horizontal to allow gravity drainage of retained water behind a slope face.
Drilling equipment is similar to anchor installation equipment.
Relief drains commonly become clogged by organic material; removal of obstructions is generally not practical — a key long-term limitation.
sections.applicability: Applies when installing relief drains to reduce water pressure behind a rock slope face, typically used in conjunction with reinforcement.

sections.title: Rock Removal
sections.summary: Describes three scales of rock removal for slope stabilization: mass excavation (drilling, blasting, heavy equipment), selective trimming of overhangs and problematic formations, and scaling to remove loose cobbles and boulders presenting rock fall hazards. Notes cost and disruption tradeoffs between mass excavation and trimming.
sections.body:
The stability of rock slopes can often be improved by the removal of material. On a large scale, such removal may take the form of mass excavation using drilling and blasting measures followed by dozers, track hoes and haul trucks.

On a smaller scale trimming may be used to more selectively remove problematic formations such as overhangs (see Figure 7-14), planes, wedges and columns. Trimming may also employ drilling and blasting and may be preferable to mass excavation in terms of cost and also in terms of potential disruption of adjacent transportation or commercial operations.

If the rock slope includes loose cobbles and boulders that may present a rock fall hazard, then scaling may be the most appropriate method of rock removal. In a scaling operation, personnel traverse the slope face while secured by ropes and harnesses. They use hand tools to dislodge rock and may even remove soil deposits and vegetation.
key_points: Mass excavation uses drilling, blasting, dozers, track hoes, and haul trucks for large-scale removal.
Trimming selectively targets overhangs, planes, wedges, and columns; may be preferred over mass excavation for cost and reduced disruption.
Scaling removes loose cobbles and boulders using rope-secured personnel with hand tools; appropriate for rock fall hazard mitigation.
Selection among mass excavation, trimming, and scaling depends on scale, hazard type, and proximity to operations.
sections.applicability: Applies when rock removal is the chosen stabilization strategy for overhangs, loose material, or overall slope geometry correction.

sections.title: Rock Fall Protection Measures
sections.summary: Covers protective measures against rock falls including surface restraints (steel face mesh as anchored panels or draping curtains), capture ditches, and catch fences along highways. Emphasizes that rock fall trajectory analysis is required to design any of these measures, and notes that computer modeling paired with videography/surveying is needed for meaningful accuracy.
sections.body:
Measures to protect against rock falls may include the installation of surface restraints, barriers or ditches. However, the design of any of these measures usually requires an assessment of the risk posed by rock falls.

Rock fall analyses are generally beyond the capabilities of hand calculations, although some graphical aids have been developed for this purpose (FHWA 1998). When the FHWA (1998) was published, the computer-supported analysis of rock falls was at a relatively early stage. The complexity of the problem was such that computer modeling had to be paired with videography and surveying to render solutions with meaningful accuracy.

After a rock fall analysis has been performed and a reasonable estimate of the final location of fallen rocks can be obtained, ditches can be designed to capture errant cobbles and boulders. Guidelines for the dimensioning of capture ditches are provided in FHWA (1998).

Steel face mesh can be installed over rock slope surfaces to restrain material that might otherwise dislodge. The mesh may be relatively fine twisted wire or it may comprise larger diameter elements depending on strength requirements. If the mesh is placed directly on the slope face, it must be secured by anchors that are installed in a regular pattern. In a separate application, the top of the mesh can be secured to a stable section of rock slope and left suspended to drape in front of the slope at lower elevations. Rocks that dislodge from the slope and would otherwise represent a rock fall hazard are intercepted by the mesh curtain. In such applications, a ditch is usually installed below the mesh to capture fallen material. As with reinforcement anchors, steel mesh is subject to corrosion in aggressive electrochemical environments. Both the mesh and its anchor components should be designed with corrosion protection.

Catch fences have become a common feature along highways that pass through mountainous terrain. In general, they are a practical and cost-effective measure to protect against rock falls. However, an assessment of rock fall trajectories is essential to determine both the proper location, height, and structural capacities of such barriers.
key_points: Rock fall protection options include surface mesh, capture ditches, and catch fences.
Rock fall trajectory analysis is required before designing any protection measure; hand calculations have limited applicability.
Computer modeling paired with videography and surveying is needed for accurate rock fall analysis.
Steel face mesh can be anchored directly to the slope face or draped from a stable upper anchor point; a catch ditch below intercepts fallen material.
Catch fences are practical and cost-effective for highway rock fall protection; proper location, height, and capacity depend on trajectory analysis.
Steel mesh and anchors are subject to corrosion in aggressive electrochemical environments and require corrosion protection.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing rock fall protection measures such as mesh, ditches, or catch fences for slopes threatening roads or infrastructure.

sections.title: Rock Sheds and Tunnels
sections.summary: Describes rock sheds as a highly effective but costly last-resort protection for vehicular traffic on hillside roadways, with a downhill-sloping roof supported by benches uphill and columns downhill. Notes that tunnels may be required where rock sheds are impractical, referencing a Canadian railway example in FHWA (1998).
sections.body:
Rock sheds are an effective method of protecting vehicular traffic from rock falls, but their use is rarely justified unless the cost of other mitigation measures is especially high. They are typically needed on roadways that have been cut into hillsides. They are designed with a roof that slopes downhill. On the uphill side of the roof, the roof support beams are secured onto benches. On the downhill side of the roof, the roof support beams can be supported by columns.

In locations where it is not practical to construct a rock shed it may be necessary to construct a tunnel. FHWA (1998) describe such an example for a railway in Canada.
key_points: Rock sheds protect vehicular traffic from rock falls but are rarely cost-justified unless other measures are too expensive.
Rock shed roofs slope downhill; uphill beams are bench-supported and downhill beams are column-supported.
Tunnels are a last-resort alternative where rock sheds are impractical.
FHWA (1998) provides a Canadian railway tunnel example for reference.
sections.applicability: Applies when rock falls pose a severe and persistent hazard to a roadway cut into a hillside and other mitigation measures are cost-prohibitive.

sections.title: Suggested Reading
sections.summary: A curated bibliography of foundational and advanced references for slope stability topics covered in Chapter 7, organized by subject area: Stability Analysis (General), Limit Equilibrium Methods, Progressive Failure, Back Analysis, Geosynthetic Reinforcement, Seismic Slope Stability, Staged Construction of Slopes, and Residual/Fully-Softened Conditions. Key authors include Bishop, Janbu, Skempton, Seed, and Ladd.
sections.body:
Topic | Reference

Stability Analysis - General
Bishop, A. W. and Bjerrum, L. (1960). The relevance of the triaxial test to the solution of stability problems, Proceedings of the ASCE Research Conference on the Shear Strength of Cohesive Soils, Boulder, CO.
Skempton, A. W. (1948). The Φ = 0 analysis of stability and its theoretical basis, Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering, Rotterdam, Vol. 1, pp. 72–78.
Terzaghi, K. Peck, R. B., and Mesri, G. (1996). Soil Mechanics in Engineering Practice, 3rd ed., Wiley, Hoboken, NJ, 549 pages.

Limit Equilibrium Methods
Bishop, A. W. (1955). The use of slip circles in the stability analysis of earth slopes, Geotechnique, 5(1), 7–17.
Bromhead, E. N. (1992). The Stability of Slopes, 2nd ed., Blackie, New York.
Janbu, N. (1954a). Application of composite slip surface for stability analysis, Proceedings of the European Conference on Stability of Earth Slopes, Stockholm, Vol. 3, pp. 43–49.
Janbu, N. (1954b). Stability Analysis of Slopes with Dimensionless Parameters, Harvard Soil Mechanics Series 46, Harvard University Press, Cambridge MA.
Janbu, N. (1968). Slope stability computations, Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering Report, The Technical University of Norway, Trondheim.

Progressive Failure
Bjerrum, L. (1967). Progressive failure in slopes of overconsolidated plastic clay and clay shales, ASCE, Journal of the Soil Mechanics and Foundation Division, 93(5), 1–49.

Back Analysis
Chandler, R. J. (1977). Back analysis techniques for slope stabilization works: a case record, Geotechnique, 27(4), 479–495.
Filz, G. M., Brandon, T. L., and Duncan, J. M. (1992). Back Analysis of Olmsted Landslide Using Anisotropic Strengths, Transportation Research Record 1343, Transportation Research Board, National Research Council, National Academy Press, Washington, DC, pp. 72–78.

Geosynthetic Reinforcement
Koerner, R. M. (1998). Designing with Geosynthetics, 4th ed., Prentice Hall, Upper Saddle River, NJ.

Seismic Slope Stability
Makdisi, F. I., and Seed, H. B. (1978). A simplified procedure for estimating dam and embankment earthquake–induced deformations, ASCE, Journal of the Geotechnical Engineering Division, 104(7), 849–867.
Seed, H. B. (1979). Considerations in the earthquake–resistant design of earth and rockfill dams, Nineteenth Rankine Lecture, Geotechnique, 29(3), 215–263.

Staged Construction of Slopes
Ladd, C. C. (1991). Stability evaluation during staged construction, ASCE, Journal of Geotechnical Engineering, 117, 540–615.

Residual and Fully-Softened Conditions
Skempton, A. W. (1977). Slope stability of cuttings in brown London clay, Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Soil Mechanics, Tokyo, Vol. 3, pp. 261–270.
Skempton, A. W. (1985). Residual strength of clays in landslides, flooded strata and the laboratory, Geotechnique, 35(1), 3–18.
key_points: General stability analysis references include foundational works by Bishop & Bjerrum (1960), Skempton (1948), and Terzaghi, Peck & Mesri (1996).
Limit equilibrium methods are addressed by Bishop (1955) on slip circles and three seminal Janbu references (1954a, 1954b, 1968) covering composite slip surfaces and dimensionless parameters.
Progressive failure in overconsolidated plastic clays and clay shales is covered by Bjerrum (1967).
Back analysis references include Chandler (1977) and Filz, Brandon & Duncan (1992) on anisotropic strength back-analysis of a real landslide.
Geosynthetic reinforcement design is referenced via Koerner (1998), Designing with Geosynthetics, 4th ed.
Seismic slope stability references include Makdisi & Seed (1978) on earthquake-induced deformations and Seed (1979) on earthquake-resistant design of earth and rockfill dams.
Staged construction stability is covered by Ladd (1991); residual and fully-softened conditions by Skempton (1977, 1985).
sections.applicability: Applies when practitioners seek foundational or supplemental literature on slope stability analysis methods, seismic considerations, progressive failure, back analysis, geosynthetics, staged construction, or residual strength conditions.

sections.title: Notation
sections.summary: Defines all symbols and notation used throughout Chapter 7 on slope stability and related topics. Covers variables for slice geometry, shear strength parameters, safety factors, geosynthetic reinforcement properties, pore pressure, rock block mechanics, seepage forces, wedge failure analysis, and Greek-letter symbols for stress, friction angles, dip, and inclination.
sections.body:
Symbol | Description
bi | Width of the slice
c | Total stress cohesion
C | Number of surfaces on which pullout resistance is mobilized
cʹ | Effective stress cohesion
F | Factor of safety
Fm | Factor of safety for Bishop's Simplified Method in effective stress example
FN | Component of W that acts perpendicular to the rock block sliding plane
FR | Factor of safety for geosynthetic strength
FS | Component of W that acts parallel to the rock block sliding plane
FW | Factor of safety against wedge failure
F∗ | Pullout resistance factor
Hi | Average height of the slice
i | Hydraulic gradient
K | Wedge factor
Le | Length of reinforcement embedded behind the trial failure surface
MARV | Minimum average roll value
Mα | Denominator in equation for calculating normal force at the base of a slice used for assessing validity of normal force
Pr | Geosynthetic reinforcement's resistance to pullout
RFCR | Reduction factor for creep
RFD | Reduction factor for durability
RFID | Reduction factor for installation damage
ru | Pore pressure coefficient
s | Shear strength
S | Seepage force
SRF | Strength reduction factor
ssu | Undrained steady state shear strength
su | Undrained shear strength
Tal | Geosynthetic's long-term tensile strength
TULT | Ultimate tensile strength of the geosynthetic based on the MARV
u | Pore water pressure
U | Uplift force applied by water at the failure plane
V | Force applied by water in the tension crack
W | Rock block weight
Wi | Weight of each slice
α | Dip direction or dip azimuth
α | Scale correction factor to account for nonlinear stress reduction
αi | Angle between the tangent to the failure surface and the horizontal
γ | Unit weight
γw | Unit weight of water
δ | Effective soil-geosynthetic interface friction angle
θ | Face angle
σ | Total stress
σʹ | Effective stress
σʹv | Effective vertical stress
τ | Shear stress required for equilibrium
φʹ | Effective stress friction angle
φ | Total stress friction angle
φʹr | Residual friction angle
Ψ | Dip
ΨFi | Inclination of the slope face as measured at right angles to the line of intersection in a wedge failure analysis
Ψi | Dip of the line of intersection in a wedge failure analysis
ΨP | Angle of a sliding block plane with respect to horizontal
key_points: Defines safety factor variants: F (general), Fm (Bishop's Simplified), FR (geosynthetic strength), FW (wedge failure).

Geosynthetic-specific symbols include Tal (long-term tensile strength), TULT (ultimate tensile strength based on MARV), Pr (pullout resistance), Le (embedment length), and reduction factors RFCR, RFD, RFID.
Rock block mechanics symbols: FN (force perpendicular to sliding plane), FS (force parallel to sliding plane), W (block weight), U (uplift force), V (tension crack water force).
Pore pressure represented by both u (pore water pressure) and ru (pore pressure coefficient); seepage captured by S (seepage force) and i (hydraulic gradient).
Greek symbols cover stress state (σ, σʹ, σʹv, τ), friction angles (φ, φʹ, φʹr), unit weights (γ, γw), and wedge/dip geometry (Ψ, ΨFi, Ψi, ΨP, αi).
Symbol α is used for two distinct quantities: dip direction/azimuth and scale correction factor for nonlinear stress reduction.
MARV (Minimum Average Roll Value) is defined here as it underpins the TULT geosynthetic strength parameter.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever interpreting symbols and notation used in Chapter 7 equations, figures, and tables covering slope stability, geosynthetic reinforcement, rock block sliding, and wedge failure analysis.
